query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing treatment conducted immediately after rapid solidification refines the lamellar spacing and enhances coherent bonding between the fcc and B2 phases in eutectic HEAs, resulting in simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a dual-phase, lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of approximately 2 μm.
generation.intervention: A rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing treatment applied post-rapid solidification.
generation.conditions: Performed under ambient service conditions typical for structural applications; the treatment should be executed immediately after the initial rapid solidification phase to allow microstructural reorganization.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing and improved coherent interphase (fcc/B2) bonding.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature annealing accelerates atomic mobility, allowing reduction in lamellar spacing (thus increasing strength via a Hall-Petch effect) and promoting the formation of coherent interfaces between phases, which improves strain transfer and accommodation, thereby enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy is expected to exhibit a statistically significant increase in tensile yield strength along with an increase or preservation of ductility (strain-to-failure).
generation.baseline: The originally as-cast eutectic HEA with typical high strength–ductility trade-offs, characterized by a 2 μm inter-lamellar spacing and standard dislocation behavior that limits simultaneous property enhancement.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for eutectic HEAs with a similar dual-phase lamellar microstructure under processing conditions that allow controlled high-temperature exposure and rapid cooling. It may not apply to non-eutectic or markedly compositionally different HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in strength and ductility remains uncertain and is likely sensitive to precise annealing temperature, time, and cooling rate. There may also be compositional dependencies that affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples from the same batch of as-cast eutectic HEA. Subject one group to the rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing treatment, and use the second group as the as-cast baseline. Conduct identical tensile tests and microstructural analyses (using SEM/TEM) on both groups.
measurements: Interface coherence indicators (e.g., via high-resolution XRD or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility over the as-cast samples, or if microstructural assessments fail to show refined lamellar spacing and enhanced interphase bonding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) has centered on establishing a dual‐phase, fine lamellar microstructure via conventional melting and casting. In the 2014 study (PMC4145285), researchers demonstrated that an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA naturally combined high strength with decent ductility at room and elevated temperatures. Subsequent processing modifications (e.g., 8% cold rolling) further increased strength, but at the expense of ductility. Thus, while processing methods have been tweaked to refine interlamellar spacing and phase volume fractions, the classical strength–ductility trade‐off still persists.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge is how to overcome the inherent compromise: refining the lamellar microstructure to boost strength typically impairs ductility. A method is needed that simultaneously tailors the interface and microarchitecture so that dislocation motion is effectively impeded (raising strength) yet strain partitioning and compatibility between phases is maintained (preserving or even enhancing ductility).
decision.lever: A rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing treatment (post-rapid solidification) designed to refine the lamellar spacing and enhance coherent interphase bonding
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend of processing-based microstructural tuning in eutectic HEAs. By applying a tailored thermal treatment, the microstructure could reorganize into a more hierarchically ordered state with ultrafine lamellae and superior interface characteristics. The refined spacing would strengthen the material via a Hall-Petch effect, while improved interfacial coherence would allow better strain accommodation and improved ductility. This lever specifically addresses the open question and inherent trade-off by attacking the microstructure architecture rather than altering composition.
